name: SOA
label: Dischord
lede: Henry Garfield paid for Dischord's second record out of his wages as a Georgetown ice cream manager, and the band was finished before its first birthday.

eras.title: The roadie takes the mic
eras.text: Henry Garfield spent 1980 hauling gear for The Teen Idles and scooping ice cream in Georgetown. When Minor Threat took guitarist Lyle Preslar from the Extorts, the three players left behind went looking for a singer and landed on the roadie who never missed a show.

years.h: A Teen Idles roadie sings at rehearsal and the idea sticks
years.p: Henry Garfield is carrying amps for [[The Teen Idles|84e8d8bf-da21-4488-89e5-50a4c12ff4fa]] when singer Nathan Strejcek misses a practice, and Garfield talks the band into letting him sing. It's a rehearsal, not a gig.
years.xp:
Jeff Nelson of the Teen Idles remembered Garfield as someone who "essentially was a roadie, and helped us schlep equipment around." Simon Jacobsen said he was at every Teen Idles show.

That summer Garfield went on the Teen Idles' California trip as one of six people in the van. The take in Los Angeles was $15 and in San Francisco $11.

years.src: WJLA: An incomplete oral history · Dischord: SOA
years.h: The Extorts find their singer behind an ice cream counter
years.p: Simon Jacobsen, on Garfield. [[Lyle Preslar|c1b9b78e-691f-424d-8ce1-53c87c24d299]] had left the Extorts to play guitar with [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] and [[Jeff Nelson|51f7994c-949d-4dbe-89eb-2c33f42a5620]] in [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]], so Jacobsen, [[Michael Hampton|4ed83c42-6348-4368-903e-9116bfa49b8e]] and Wendel Blow needed a singer.
years.xp:
They sent MacKaye as go-between, and the meeting happened at the Häagen-Dazs on Wisconsin Avenue in Georgetown, where Garfield was a manager. By Jacobsen's account it lasted "all of five minutes," with Garfield taking notes on scraps of paper.

After that it was practice every other day: parents' basements, Dischord House, even rooms in Kalorama mansions. Hampton said later that Garfield always charmed the moms.

years.cap: Handwritten flyer for a December 13, 1980 benefit with SOA, Minor Threat and the Untouchables
years.h: SOA debut in December, and the scene's sound gets harder
years.p: Dischord's own history says SOA brought a new level of aggression to D.C. music, a close match for the mood of the younger kids.

years.h: Two nights at d.c. space for the Unheard Music Festival
years.p: The downtown arts space hosts SOA on both nights, in the band's first month on stage.

eras.title: Ice cream money and a one-way ticket
eras.text: SOA lasted about as long as a school year. In that time they made Dischord's second record, paid for by Garfield, and played their last show on the night Garfield first sang with Black Flag, the band that took him to California.

years.h: SOA play the 9:30 Club on F Street with Minor Threat on the bill
years.p: One of the handful of shows SOA ever played. A 12-minute set from that night survives on video.

years.src: Dischord: SOA, No Policy · Wikipedia: No Policy · WJLA: An incomplete oral history
years.h: No Policy: Dischord No. 2, paid for with ice cream money
years.p: Ten songs on a seven-inch, recorded at Inner Ear with Skip Groff. Garfield covered the recording and the pressing himself.
years.xp:
Tina Angelos shot the cover photo, and Michael Hampton and Chris Edwards designed the sleeve.

Dischord was one record old, with The Teen Idles' Minor Disturbance as No. 1, and had no money for a second. Garfield had a steady paycheck from Häagen-Dazs. Jeff Nelson later said the Georgetown store manager funded Dischord's second record.

The session work ran from December 1980 into January 1981. The EP is long out of vinyl print, but Dischord has kept the songs in circulation on compilations ever since.

yt: Live at the Wilson Center, April 4, 1981
years.h: Ivor Hanson, an admiral's son, takes over the drums
years.p: [[Ivor Hanson|a17981f7-ab3d-46dc-859a-582ac894cb20]] replaces Simon Jacobsen. His father is a U.S. Navy admiral, so SOA rehearse at the Naval Observatory. By Hanson's own count he plays exactly one show with the band.

years.big: "Henry's last show with S.O.A. was his first show with Black Flag."
years.src: Dischord: SOA · WJLA: An incomplete oral history · Wikipedia: State of Alert
years.h: SOA's last show: Philadelphia, opening for [[Black Flag|9941a936-196a-4a62-ae53-a69cbc33f20e]]
years.p: Drummer Ivor Hanson, on the night Henry Garfield opened with SOA and then sang with Black Flag. It ended in a riot, and SOA broke up that month.
years.xp:
Dischord's history records the riot plainly. Hanson remembered it starting when local residents slashed someone, with bottles and bricks thrown.

It was one of only a handful of SOA shows. Hampton put the total at about five; Wikipedia counts about a dozen.

years.cap: Henry Rollins singing with Black Flag, 1983
years.src: Wikipedia: Henry Rollins · WJLA: An incomplete oral history
years.h: Garfield quits the ice cream job and becomes Henry Rollins
years.p: After a Black Flag audition at Tu Casa Studio, he takes the surname Rollins and plays his first official show with the band at the Cuckoo's Nest in Costa Mesa, California, on July 25.
years.xp:
Garfield had been a Black Flag fan since getting the Nervous Breakdown EP. Before the audition, Dez Cadena let him sing Clocked In with the band at a New York bar show.

Rollins was a name he and [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] had used as teenagers.

years.h: Hampton and Hanson start [[Faith|f735a867-9a16-451f-8f83-669ed42e2574]] with Alec MacKaye and Chris Bald
years.p: With Garfield gone west, [[Michael Hampton|4ed83c42-6348-4368-903e-9116bfa49b8e]] and Hanson keep playing together, through Faith and then [[Embrace|9d1ad8e3-8740-429a-bdc5-52f96a9c4431]].

eras.title: The records outlive the band
eras.text: SOA were gone before most of D.C. had heard them on vinyl. Dischord kept the songs moving anyway, first on the sampler that mapped the early scene, then on a 12-inch that gathered the label's first singles.

years.h: Three SOA songs land on Flex Your Head
years.p: I Hate the Kids, Disease and Stepping Stone Party sit on Dischord's compilation of early D.C. bands, next to [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]], [[The Teen Idles|84e8d8bf-da21-4488-89e5-50a4c12ff4fa]] and [[Void|960a1d2f-2b5f-4fcf-bf11-4957529a6508]].

years.cap: Henry Rollins on stage with Black Flag, Berlin, June 10, 1984
years.h: No Policy goes onto a 12-inch with the label's other early singles
years.p: Dischord puts SOA's seven-inch on Four Old 7"s on a 12", three years after the band split and Garfield became Rollins.

eras.title: The vault opens
eras.text: Once Dischord started mining its own history, SOA kept coming back into print. The last surprise was the band's first recording session, released more than three decades after it was taped.

years.p: Dischord 1981: The Year in Seven Inches collects the record with the label's other singles from that year.

years.h: Public Defender gets a slot in the 20 Years box
years.p: Dischord picks the SOA song for 20 Years of Dischord, the label's anniversary box.

years.src: Dischord: SOA, First Demo · Discogs: SOA, First Demo
years.h: A 1980 session waits 33 years for its release
years.p: SOA recorded eight songs with Skip Groff at Inner Ear on December 29, 1980. Two takes went on Flex Your Head and one on No Policy; the full session finally comes out on colored vinyl.
years.xp: Five of the eight songs had never been heard in these versions. The first SOA recording became the last SOA release.
